passage: It was nearly ten, and the only light in the village was the one under Faiz's door. His father, Imran, stood outside it for a long time, holding a steel glass of warm milk. Earlier he had shouted in front of the neighbours about Faiz wanting to go to the district cricket trials in town. Now he knocked. "Faiz, can I come in?" A pause. "Okay." Imran sat on the edge of the charpai. "I was scared, and I said it badly. You're my only son and the town is far. Can you tell me what you want, and then I'll tell you what worries me?" Faiz looked up, surprised. Slowly, he started talking about the trials.

qa.q: What was Imran holding outside Faiz's door?
qa.a: He was holding a steel glass of warm milk.

qa.q: How can you tell Faiz did not expect his father to soften?
qa.a: He looked up surprised when his father admitted being scared, and only then slowly started talking.

qa.q: Why is Imran's knock a turning point?
qa.a: By admitting his fear and offering to listen first, Imran showed Faiz respect, which made Faiz willing to share instead of staying shut in.

qa.q: How might Faiz see his father differently after tonight?
qa.a: He might see him as someone who can admit mistakes and wants to hear him, which may make him more willing to listen back.

grounding: It shows a parent knocking later, admitting fear and poor words, and offering to listen to what the son wants, modelling the respect he wants back.

passage: The London flat still felt stiff from the afternoon's argument. Chidi had stormed off when his mother, Jin, refused to let him take the late train to the music festival in Bristol. Around nine, Jin made two mugs of hot chocolate and knocked on his door. "Chidi? Can I come in?" He shrugged. She sat on his desk chair. "I was scared earlier, and I said it badly. That wasn't fair to you." Chidi kept his eyes on his guitar. "Can we talk properly? What you want, and what worries me. I'll listen first." Chidi turned slowly. "Really?" "Really." He took a mug. For the first time that day, his shoulders came down.

qa.q: Where did Chidi want to take the late train to?
qa.a: He wanted to take it to the music festival in Bristol.

qa.q: What does Chidi's shoulders coming down suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt relieved and respected once his mother admitted she had been scared and offered to listen first. 😊

qa.q: What made Jin's approach work after the fight?
qa.a: She went to Chidi first, owned her fear and harsh words, and offered to hear what he wanted before deciding, which opened a real conversation.

qa.q: What would change if Jin had waited for Chidi to apologise first?
qa.a: The silence might have lasted much longer, with each waiting for the other, and the festival question would stay a fight.

grounding: It illustrates a parent softening first, admitting fear and harsh words and offering to listen before deciding, which models respect for her son.

passage:
Jagdish drove four hours to the boarding school in Dehradun on Saturday morning, after a phone call on Thursday that had ended with his son Darshan hanging up on him.

They'd fought about Darshan wanting to drop science for arts. Jagdish had said, "Out of the question. I won't discuss it." Darshan had said, "You never listen," and cut the call.

In the visitors' room, Darshan sat stiffly, arms crossed.

Jagdish took a breath. "Beta, I was scared on the phone, and I said it badly. I'm sorry. I'd like to hear what you want. And then I'll tell you what worries me. Can we do that?"

Darshan looked up, surprised. "You're not going to shout?"

"No. I came to listen."

Darshan uncrossed his arms. For forty minutes, he talked about history and writing, and Jagdish listened without interrupting once.

qa.q: How far did Jagdish drive to the boarding school?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when his father apologised?
qa.a: He was surprised and a little wary, then relieved enough to uncross his arms and talk.

qa.q: Why was Jagdish's apology a strong first step?
qa.a: He admitted his fear and poor words, then offered to listen before deciding, modelling the respect he wants from Darshan.

qa.q: What might Jagdish be feeling as he listens for forty minutes?
qa.a: He is probably still anxious about Darshan's future, but also determined to understand him.

grounding: At a boarding school, Jagdish softens first, admitting he was scared and spoke badly, and listens to Darshan before deciding, modelling respect.

passage:
Saurabh,

I'm sliding this under your door because I'm not sure you'll open it if I knock, and that's fair.

Last night I said you couldn't go on the cycling trip to Lonavala, and when you argued, I said, "This discussion is over." Then I said something about your marks that had nothing to do with the trip. I'm sorry.

The truth is, I was scared. Highways, trucks, a group of boys with no adult. That fear came out as shouting, and that's on me.

I'd like to try again. Can we sit down tomorrow after dinner? You tell me what you want and why it matters to you, and I'll listen properly, all the way through. Then I'll tell you what worries me, and we'll see if there's a way.

I'm not promising yes. But I'm promising to listen first.

Papa (Amandeep)

qa.q: Where was the cycling trip going?
qa.a: To Lonavala.

qa.q: What feeling does Amandeep say was really behind the shouting?
qa.a: Amandeep says it was fear, about highways, trucks and no adult with the group, and that fear came out as shouting.

qa.q: Why is listening first a strong move for Amandeep?
qa.a: It shows respect and isn't weakness; it models the respect Amandeep hopes to get back and gives father and son a chance to find a way together.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and relieved, and more willing to talk because his father apologised first.

grounding: Amandeep writes to his son admitting he was scared and spoke badly, and offers to listen first, modelling the respect he hopes for.

passage:
You want to know what changed things with my son? I'm Madhav, Vikas's father, and I'll tell you straight: I knocked first.

Vikas wanted to go to a concert in Mumbai with friends. Overnight. I said no, loudly, and added a few things about his attitude. He said I treated him like a baby. Doors slammed. Two days of silence.

On the third night, I stood outside his room for about five minutes before I knocked. Then I said, "Vikas, I was scared and I said it badly. Can we talk about what you want, and what worries me?"

He opened the door, looking suspicious. I sat on his bed and let him talk. He told me about the band, the friends, the plan for where they'd stay. I didn't interrupt.

Then I told him my fear: the crowds, the late train. He actually listened. My son, who'd been rolling his eyes for months.

qa.q: Where was the concert Vikas wanted to go to?
qa.a: In Mumbai.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel standing outside Vikas's room for five minutes?
qa.a: He felt nervous and unsure, worried about how Vikas would react to him knocking first.

qa.q: What did Madhav's approach achieve?
qa.a: By apologising and listening before deciding, he got Vikas to listen to his fears too, showing respect earns respect.

qa.q: How did Vikas seem to feel when he opened the door?
qa.a: He seemed suspicious at first, then willing to talk once Madhav listened without interrupting.

grounding: Madhav, a father, softens first after a fight, admits he was scared and spoke badly, and listens before deciding, modelling the respect he wants.

passage: I was at Faiz's place that evening to finish our geography chart, so I saw most of it, though I can't say what either of them was really feeling. After the shouting at dinner, Faiz had shut himself in his room, and I was sitting on his floor with the chart paper. About an hour later there was a knock. Wasim Uncle stood in the doorway, not coming in. He said, "I was scared and I said it badly. Can we talk about what you want and what worries me?" Faiz didn't answer at first. Wasim Uncle just waited. Then Faiz said, "The concert's on Saturday. Everyone's going." Wasim Uncle nodded, asked who was driving and where it was, and didn't say no. I rolled up the chart and said I'd finish it at home. When I left, they were both sitting on the bed. I'm Yash, just the friend who happened to be there.

qa.q: Why was Yash at Faiz's place that evening?
qa.a: To finish their geography chart.

qa.q: How did Yash seem to feel on the floor when the knock came?
qa.a: Yash seems awkward and a little uneasy at being caught in a family moment, and tactful enough to leave so they could talk.

qa.q: Why did Wasim Uncle's knock work as a turning point?
qa.a: He admitted his fear and his harsh words first, then asked to hear what Faiz wanted, which invited talk instead of another fight.

qa.q: What might Faiz have felt when Wasim Uncle apologised at the door?
qa.a: Faiz may have felt surprised and wary at first, hence the silence, then relieved enough to explain about the concert.

grounding: Shows a parent softening first by admitting fear and inviting the teen to talk, as seen by a visiting friend.
